question: Why can we not use the training MSE to choose the polynomial degree?

answers.answer: It keeps decreasing with model flexibility, so the most flexible model would always win
answers.feedback: Correct! A flexible model can also fit the noise, which lowers the training MSE but not the test MSE.

answers.answer: It is always higher than the test MSE
answers.feedback: Not quite. It is usually lower than the test MSE, because the model was fitted to exactly these data.

answers.answer: It ignores the bias of the model
answers.feedback: Not quite. A model with high bias also has a high training MSE. The problem is variance, which the training MSE does not reveal.

question: In our simulation, the noise has a standard deviation of σ = 0.5. What is the lowest expected test MSE any model can reach?

answers.feedback: Correct! The irreducible error is the noise variance σ² = 0.5² = 0.25.
Not quite. 0.5 is the standard deviation, but the MSE is in squared units.
Not quite. Even a perfect model cannot predict the random noise in new observations.
Not quite. Even a perfect model is left with the irreducible error, the noise variance σ².

question: Suppose the true relationship were quadratic instead of cubic. Which polynomial degree would you expect to have the lowest test MSE?

answers.feedback: Correct! Degree 2 is the simplest model without bias. Every additional degree only adds variance.
Not quite. A straight line cannot represent a quadratic curve, so it has high bias.
Not quite. Degree 3 has no bias either, but it adds variance without any benefit.
